title: Why Are So Many Countries Suddenly Leaving the World's War Crimes Court?
summary: Have you ever felt like a referee was only calling fouls on one team? That's what some countries are saying about the International Criminal Court, or ICC. This court in The Hague, Netherlands, was set up in 2002 to put people on trial for the very worst crimes—like genocide and war crimes. But now, a bunch of countries are quitting, and it's causing a big stir. The latest is Chad, a country in northern Africa. Its military government announced it's leaving, saying the court mostly goes after African nations. Out of 13 investigations the ICC has opened, nine are in Africa, but only four are in other parts of the world—and those four haven't made much progress, Chad says. This follows Burkina Faso, Mali, and Niger, which all left in September for the same reason. Venezuela also quit last week, calling the court biased. What's behind this sudden wave? A lot of it has to do with the United States. The U.S. has never liked the ICC, but things got worse after the court issued arrest warrants for Israeli leaders in 2024. Now, the Trump administration is openly trying to weaken the court. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the U.S. would work to "systematically disable" the ICC. In fact, a U.S. official even called Chad to pressure it to leave. Critics say the withdrawals are a blow to justice for victims of atrocities. But supporters of the move say the court needs to be fair to everyone, not just pick on certain countries. It's a messy fight over who gets to decide right and wrong on the world stage.
why_it_matters: When international courts that are supposed to deliver justice are seen as unfair, it can make the world less safe, because leaders may commit crimes without fear of punishment—and that can affect peace everywhere, even in your country's future.

background_read: The ICC was set up in 2002 after many countries signed a treaty called the Rome Statute. It was meant to make sure that no one—even leaders—could escape punishment for terrible crimes.
However, the United States, China, and Russia never joined the ICC. The U.S. even passed a law to protect American citizens from being taken to the court.
For years, many African leaders have said the ICC unfairly targets their continent. Only African suspects have been put on trial so far, even though crimes happen everywhere.
Article_Structure: WHO: Chad, Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger, Venezuela, and the United States
WHAT: Several countries are quitting or trying to weaken the International Criminal Court (ICC)
WHERE: The ICC is in The Hague, Netherlands, but the withdrawals come from Africa and South America, while pressure comes from the US
WHY: These countries say the ICC is biased against African nations, and the US wants to disable it after arrest warrants for Israeli leaders

perspectives.perspective: Victims of atrocities and human rights groups
perspectives.description: They say the ICC is the last hope for justice when national courts fail. If the court is weakened, guilty leaders might escape punishment, leaving victims without any way to hold them to account.

perspectives.perspective: Government officials in African countries leaving the ICC
perspectives.description: They feel the court is one-sided because it only prosecutes Africans while ignoring crimes by powerful nations. They want a court that treats all countries equally or they would rather leave it.
